Veterinary dermatology practice wins approval for new Darien location at Old Kings Highway North
Date: Sun Apr 26 09:00:15 2026 UTC

DARIEN - A family-owned veterinary dermatology practice in Stratford is opening a location in Darien.
Unleashed Veterinary Dermatology plans to open at 50 Old Kings Highway North in a 9,000-square-foot, two-story office previously occupied by Hartford HealthCare. The practice will occupy the entire second floor of the building, while Hartford HealthCare will remain on the first floor.
The Planning & Zoning Commission on Tuesday approved a zoning change allowing specialty veterinary office uses in the business zone - uses that more closely resemble medical offices than traditional veterinary clinics. The change takes effect May 10.  It does not include veterinary hospitals, walk-in clinics, kennels, or any veterinary use requiring overnight boarding of animals.
At a March 10 public hearing, attorney Amy Zabatakis, of Rucci Law Group, said the veterinary dermatology practice functions much like a human dermatology office. 
"The patients - the companion animals - will come in. They will see a doctor. They will receive treatment. They will receive medication. They will leave," Zabatakis said.
Since a medical office previously occupied the space, only minor interior renovations are planned. No exterior building or parking area changes are proposed, and there will be no outdoor space for the animals, Zabatakis said. The layout includes six examination rooms, two procedure rooms and office space. 
Owner Elizabeth Falk founded the dermatology service at Cornell University Veterinary Specialists in Stamford in 2017. That practice closed following her departure in 2024, the same year she opened the Stratford location.
Falk said she chose Darien for the expansion in part due to an existing client base in the area.
"We already have many Darien clients, and we know how much they love their pets," Falk said. "However, we know it can be tough for dogs and cats to go on long drives. This new location will give them better access to our services and allow us to better serve the lower Fairfield and Westchester county areas," Falk said.
"With the prevalence of animal allergies rising and with our existing clinic being the only clinic in Connecticut dedicated to veterinary dermatology, we hope that many of our clients will be appreciating our new location," she said.
Specialty veterinarians are a growing area of veterinary practice, according to Medi-Tech, a global health care consulting firm. 
"The global veterinary dermatology market is set to witness a growth rate of about 9% in the next five years," Medi-Tech said. "Rising pet ownership, high and increasing prevalence of dermatological conditions, innovation in veterinary therapeutics ... are some of the key factors driving the veterinary dermatology market."
The Darien practice, similar to the Stratford practice, will be open during regular business hours. Services will include allergy testing, skin scrapings, cultures, biopsies, endocrine testing, and minor outpatient dermatologic procedures, such as laser surgery, according to the proposal.

Danbury OKs expanded building plans for west side cancer center
Date: Sun May 31 09:00:12 2026 UTC

DANBURY - The city approved expanded building plans for a $115 million cancer treatment center on the west side that is preparing to break ground after years of regulatory delay.
"(T)he applicant is proposing a minor building addition of 1,300 square feet to the basement level because the specialized proton equipment required a slightly larger support space," said Allie Smith, an associate planner with the city's professional planning and zoning department.
Smith is referring to what would be the second proton therapy cancer treatment center between New York City and Boston, after the Connecticut Proton center in Wallingford, which is scheduled to open later this year.
Proton therapy is considered advanced radiation treatment because it uses the positively charged particles to "target cancer with exceptional precision," reducing damage to nearby healthy tissue.
The expanded building plans for Danbury Proton are the latest development in a prolonged effort to serve western Connecticut and nearby New York residents with the novel cancer treatment.
The project, which was set to break ground on a 3-acre site overlooking Danbury Municipal Airport this spring, is "very busy marketing and selling the bonds," a spokesman said.
"We're ready to break ground as soon as we close on the bonds," said Drew Crandall on Friday. "We are in conversation with investors every day and we are making good progress."
In March, Danbury's City Council agreed to use its bonding power to help Danbury Proton get low-cost financing under a "conduit issuer" agreement. Around the same time, the city's Planning Commission extended approvals for the project, which were scheduled to expire in July.
All that means that Danbury Proton expects to open its 17,000-square-foot facility at 85 Wooster Heights Road in late 2027 or early 2028.
"The day is coming when we will be treating patients with revolutionary proton therapy cancer treatment," Crandall said in a newsletter to supporters last week. "Countless patients and their families will benefit from proton therapy."

Connecticut's first proton therapy center opens in Wallingford for precision cancer treatment (https://www.ctinsider.com/business/article/connecticut-proton-therapy-center-cancer-yale-hhc-22412916.php)
【turn20news11】 [wordlim: 100] Published: last month; Connecticut's first proton therapy center, the Connecticut Proton Center, has officially opened in Wallingford through a joint effort by Hartford HealthCare and Yale New Haven Health. The $70 million facility is equipped with advanced medical technology, including a massive particle accelerator used in delivering targeted radiation for cancer treatment. The innovation allows for highly precise radiation therapy, especially beneficial for treating localized tumors and pediatric cancers while minimizing long-term side effects compared to traditional chemotherapy or radiation therapies. The 25,000-square-foot center, which will be fully operational by year-end, is expected to employ around 40 people and treat up to 60 patients daily. The facility represents over a decade of collaboration between the two health systems and eliminates the need for Connecticut residents to travel to New York or Boston for proton therapy. The Wallingford location was chosen for its central access and lower electricity costs. Additionally, a second proton center is in development in Danbury, estimated at $115 million and still seeking funding. This project underscores Connecticut’s commitment to enhancing cancer care through technological innovation and cross-institutional collaboration.
Connecticut’s first proton therapy center opens in Wallingford for precision cancer treatment
Date: Tue Sep  1 19:22:44 2026 UTC

WALLINGFORD - Connecticut's two largest hospital systems teamed up on Tuesday to open a new $70 million facility in Wallingford that will offer proton therapy, a precision cancer treatment requiring hundreds of tons of specialized equipment, including its own particle accelerator.
The CEOs of Hartford HealthCare and Yale New Haven Health joined employees and elected officials to cut the ribbon on the Connecticut Proton Center at 932 Northrop Road, near Interstate 91. 
"This is unique; it's done right so that we didn't have a proton war in this state," said Chris Chandler, CEO of Proton International, the project's developer. "People came together and did the right thing to bring this technology to their people, so I applaud you and I thank you for that."
The two health systems joined forces so patients who need proton therapy would not have to travel to Boston or New York for treatment, Hartford HealthCare CEO Jeffrey Flaks said. 
Proton therapy is particularly valuable in treating children with cancer, who can suffer serious, lifelong side effects from chemotherapy and less targeted radiation, said Dr. Charles Rutter, a radiation oncologist with Hartford HealthCare.  
"X-ray-based treatment delivers radiation therapy precisely to a target, but there is some dose beyond that target," Rutter said. "With proton radiation therapy, protons interact with tissue differently; they deposit dose within the target, and beyond that target, they no longer exist."
A massive cyclotron, or particle accelerator, was built as part of the center to create the protons used in treatment. The accelerator, along with a system of magnets, concrete shielding and wiring, occupies a significant portion of the 25,000-square-foot building.
The treatment system includes a table controlled by a robotic arm that can rotate in multiple directions, as well as a massive gantry that positions the proton beam. Employees said a crane was needed to install the equipment.
Plans for a dedicated proton center in Connecticut were first proposed in 2007 and announced publicly in 2019. The project later received state approval through the Certificate of Need process, which determines whether a new medical facility is needed.
Contractors started work on the project in October 2024, breaking ground on 12 acres of undeveloped vacant land along the interstate.  
The Wallingford site was chosen in part because of the central location and access to relatively inexpensive electricity supplied by the town's power company, which offers rates up to 40% less than large utility firms, officials have said.
The city of Danbury approved plans for second proton center in the state earlier this year, at a projected cost of $115 million. That project was still seeking funding through bond issues as of late May.

CVS pharmacies across Connecticut now fill prescriptions for cats and dogs
Date: Wed Jul 22 14:04:27 2026 UTC

Drug store giant CVS Health is expanding further into the pet care business, announcing Wednesday that its pharmacies now fill common prescriptions for cats and dogs.
The Rhode Island-based retailer said all 9,000 CVS Pharmacy locations nationwide, including about 180 in Connecticut, can now dispense many medications commonly prescribed by veterinarians, including antibiotics, insulin, pain relievers and treatments for allergies and flea and tick prevention.
Pet prescriptions will be eligible for many of the same services available to human patients, including automatic refills, prescription synchronization and, for some medications, home delivery.

During Cusano's tenure Stamford Health System acquired the neighboring St. Joseph Medical Center and constructed the Tully Family Wellness Center on the former St. Joseph site. It was also during this time the SHS entered into a major teaching affiliation with the Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons.

From 1994 to 2000, the hospital had significant financial difficulties, but the hospital's finances began to improve under CEO Brian Grissler, with revenues in 2007 of $357 million.

In 2008, the hospital announced plans to expand its rooms and several departments. The expansion of the hospital, dubbed "New Stamford Hospital", resulted in an 11-story glass structure. The expansion was completed in late 2016 and cost approximately $575 million.

Stamford Health has expanded since 2010 with an affiliated medical staff called Stamford Health Medical Group.[citation needed] Also since 2010, Stamford Health has opened small outpatient clinical, laboratory and imaging facilities throughout Fairfield County and southwestern Connecticut.
